Advice for victims

New Zealand Police have an important role responding to crime and supporting victims. This page outlines what victims can expect from Police, our responsibilities and where further support is available.

Overview

This page helps you check whether victim information is relevant to your situation, understand key rights and Police’s role, and find the right next step where more information or action is needed.

If it's an emergency, call 111

For non-emergency reporting, use 105. For urgent but not life-threatening road incidents, call *555.

Call 111

Who is a victim?

A victim of crime is someone who has been directly affected by a crime.

This can include situations where:

  • A crime was committed against you.
  • You were physically hurt because of a crime.
  • Your property was taken or damaged because of a crime.
  • You are the parent or guardian of a child or young person affected by a crime.
  • You are an immediate family member of someone who died or is unable to act for themselves because of a crime.

You may still be a victim even if you do not report to Police.

Your rights as a victim

As a victim of crime, you have rights in the justice process. These can include how you are treated, information you may receive, access to services, and ways to have your views considered.

This section outlines rights that may apply at different stages.

1

When you report

You can expect to be treated with respect and compassion, and to receive information about services and support that may be available.

2

During investigation

You can be kept informed about your case by Police where possible during the investigation.

3

At court

You can have rights connected to court processes, including having your views considered at some points where the law allows.

4

At sentencing

You can choose whether to make a . The court can consider this when deciding the sentence, and can order in some cases.

Learn more about Victim Impact StatementsLearn more about reparation
5

After sentencing

Eligible victims can apply for the and may receive certain updates after sentencing. Some victims can also make submissions to the .

Learn more about the Victim Notification RegisterLearn more about the Parole Board

At any time

You can seek support, give feedback, or make a complaint at any time.

Get supportGive feedback or make a complaint

Learn more about victims’ rights

For more information about victims’ rights, read the Victims’ Rights Act 2002 and the Victims Code 2015.

Victims' Rights Act 2002Victims Code 2015

The role of Police

Police work to prevent crime and crashes, improve public safety, maintain law and order, and bring offenders to account.

This section explains the role of Police, the types of help Police can provide, and what may not be Police responsibility.

Receive and record your report
Police can receive and record reports or information about what happened.
Report a crime
Assess what response may be needed
Police can assess the information and work out what response is needed.
What happens next
Investigate where appropriate
Police can investigate where appropriate, depending on the situation and available information.
Lay charges and prosecute where evidence allows
Police can take action where legal and evidential thresholds are met.
Keep you informed and updated on your case
Police can provide information about your case where possible, while considering privacy, safety, legal, and investigation reasons.
Connect you with support services
Police can connect you with support or other services where appropriate.
